name: Odyssey Voyage
lines: Hide in the wooden horse, keep silent, and open the gates of Troy
Splinter of the wooden horse
A pale sliver of fir from the horse's flank, from the night the war ended.

Homer never tells the whole story of the horse in one place: Helen remembers it in Book 4, and the bard Demodocus sings it in Book 8. The fuller telling is in Virgil's Aeneid, written about 700 years later.
Inside the horse a soldier called Anticlus wanted to answer Helen when she called in his wife's voice. Odysseus held his mouth shut until she went away.

On the way home, Odysseus' fleet raided Ismarus, the town of the Cicones, and stayed too long feasting; the Cicones came back with their neighbours and the Greeks lost men from every ship (Book 9). It was the first of many delays.
Find your three scouts who ate the lotus, and bring them back to the ship
Pressed lotus flower
A flower from the Lotus-Eaters' groves, pressed flat. Its scent still makes you forget what you were doing.
Odysseus sent three men inland to find out who lived there. The Lotus-Eaters meant them no harm; they simply shared their food.
Whoever tasted the honey-sweet fruit no longer wanted to bring news or go home. Odysseus dragged them back weeping, tied them under the benches, and sailed before anyone else could taste it.
Outwit Polyphemus in his cave, and get out alive
Tuft of ram's fleece
Thick, curly wool from the belly of the Cyclops' great ram, where you clung on.
Odysseus brought a goatskin of very strong dark wine, a gift from Maron, a priest he had spared at Ismarus. The Cyclops drank three bowls of it.
When the other Cyclopes heard Polyphemus roar and asked who was hurting him, he shouted 'Nobody!' and they went home.
As his ship pulled away, Odysseus could not resist shouting his real name. Polyphemus prayed to his father Poseidon, and that curse is why the voyage home took ten years.
Take the bag of winds from Aeolus, then stay awake all the way home
Silver cord from the bag of winds
The shining cord that tied the ox-hide bag shut. Hold it to your ear and you can hear a breeze.
Aeolus gave Odysseus every stormy wind, tied in an ox-hide bag with a silver cord, and sent a gentle west wind to blow him home.

For nine days and nights Odysseus held the sail ropes himself. On the tenth day, with the fires of Ithaca in sight, he fell asleep. His crew opened the bag, sure it held gold, and the storm winds blew them all the way back to Aeolia.
Aeolus refused to help again: a man the gods hated so much, he said, must not be helped.
The Harbour of the Giants
Choose where to moor at Telepylus, and escape the giants' boulders
Pebble from the giants' harbour
A smooth grey pebble, chipped off one of the boulders the Laestrygonians threw.
Eleven of Odysseus' twelve ships sailed into the calm harbour, ringed by cliffs. Odysseus alone tied his ship to a rock outside its mouth.
The Laestrygonians, giants, gathered on the cliffs and smashed the ships with boulders. Only Odysseus' ship, outside, got away; he cut the cable with his sword and his men rowed for their lives.
Win back your crew from Circe, without joining her menagerie yourself
Black root, white flower. Hermes said it was hard for mortals to dig; you managed it.

Circe welcomed Odysseus' scouts with cheese, barley, honey and wine, and a drug in it; one tap of her wand and they were pigs, though their minds stayed their own. Only Eurylochus stayed outside and ran back to tell.

On the way to rescue them, Odysseus met Hermes, looking like a young man, who gave him the herb moly. Circe's potion did nothing to him; she swore an oath and turned his men back, younger and taller and handsomer than before.
They stayed with her a whole year, feasting.
Speaking with the Dead
Pour the offerings, hold back the shades, and hear Tiresias first
Poplar leaf from Persephone's grove
A silvery leaf from the grove at the edge of the world. It never quite turns brown.
Circe told Odysseus to sail to the edge of the world, dig a pit and pour offerings for the dead: milk and honey, then sweet wine, then water, with white barley sprinkled over.

The first shade to come was Elpenor, a young crewman who had fallen from Circe's roof; he asked to be buried properly, and Odysseus promised. Then came his own mother, Anticleia, whom he had not known was dead. He held her back, weeping, until Tiresias had drunk.
Tiresias warned him: leave the Sun's cattle unharmed and you may all reach home; harm them, and you will come home late, alone, in a stranger's ship, to trouble in your house.
Stop your crew's ears, be tied to the mast, and hear the song as you pass
A soft, honey-smelling plug of beeswax. Your crew needed it more than you did.
Circe told Odysseus how to pass the Sirens. He softened a cake of beeswax in the sun, stopped his men's ears with it, and had them tie him upright to the mast.
When he heard the song he begged to be untied. Perimedes and Eurylochus only tied him tighter, and the crew rowed on until the singing faded.
Scylla and Charybdis
Sail the strait between Scylla's cliff and Charybdis' whirlpool
Whorled shell from the strait
A spiral shell, twisted like the water in Charybdis.
Circe said: pass close to Scylla's cliff, because it is better to lose six men than the whole ship. Do not stop to fight her.
Odysseus put on his armour and took two spears anyway, and stood at the bow watching for her. He never saw her coming. Six heads swept down and took six of his best men.
Later, shipwrecked, he drifted back to Charybdis on a broken mast and saved himself by leaping up and clinging like a bat to the fig tree above the whirlpool until she spat his timbers out again.
The Cattle of the Sun
Keep your crew fed for a month of contrary winds, and leave the Sun's cattle alone
A tuft of golden hair caught on a thorn where the Sun's cattle graze. Not one of them was harmed for it.
The south wind blew for a whole month. When the ship's food ran out, the men fished and hunted birds with bent hooks, and still they starved.

Odysseus went inland to pray and fell asleep. Eurylochus persuaded the crew to kill the best of the cattle, promising the Sun a temple at home. The hides crept along the ground and the meat lowed on the spits.
When they sailed, Zeus struck the ship with a thunderbolt. Only Odysseus lived, clinging to the keel and mast, and drifted nine days to Calypso's island.
Choose home over forever, build a raft, and survive Poseidon's storm
Peg from your raft
A wooden peg, smoothed by an adze, from the raft you built yourself. The rest of it is driftwood now.
Calypso kept Odysseus seven years and offered to make him immortal and ageless. He sat on the shore every day, weeping for home.
Zeus sent Hermes to tell her to let him go. She gave him a bronze axe, an adze and augers, and showed him where the tall dry trees grew. He felled twenty and built the raft in four days.
On the eighteenth day at sea Poseidon saw him and raised a storm. The sea-goddess Ino gave him her veil to tie round himself, and he swam for two days and nights to the coast of Scheria.
Win the Phaeacians' help: Nausicaa, the queen, the games and your story
A heavy stone discus from the games of the Phaeacians. Yours went further than theirs.
Nausicaa told Odysseus to go to the palace and clasp the knees of her mother, Queen Arete, not her father: if the queen liked him, he would get home.
A young Phaeacian called Euryalus mocked him at the games. Odysseus picked up a discus bigger than any of theirs and threw it past every mark.
When Demodocus sang of the wooden horse, Odysseus wept, and told them who he was. The Phaeacians carried him home in one night, asleep, with their gifts.
Come home in disguise, string the great bow, and win back your house
Arrow of the twelve axes
A long arrow with grey goose feathers. It flew through the rings of twelve axes and never touched one.
Athena disguised Odysseus as an old beggar. He stayed with Eumaeus, his loyal swineherd, and there made himself known to his son Telemachus.
Old Eurycleia, his nurse, knew him by the scar on his leg, from a boar hunt in his youth, when she washed his feet. He made her keep silent.
Penelope set the contest: whoever could string Odysseus' bow and shoot through twelve axes would marry her. None of the suitors could even string it. Odysseus did it sitting on his stool.
Penelope tested him last: she told the maid to move their bed. Only Odysseus knew it could not be moved, because he had built it round the trunk of a living olive tree.
Telemachus at Pylos
As Telemachus: join Nestor's feast, mind your manners, and ask about your father
A little jar of the pale sand of sandy Pylos, from the shore where the bulls were offered.
Telemachus was guided by Athena, disguised as Mentor, an old friend of the family. He was shy of speaking to so famous a king; she told him the words would come.
Nestor's son Peisistratus offered the cup first to Mentor, as the elder of the two guests.
Nestor had no news of Odysseus, but told how the Greeks had scattered on the way home from Troy, and sent Telemachus on to Menelaus by chariot, with Peisistratus to drive.
The Hall of Menelaus
As Telemachus: be welcomed by Menelaus and Helen, choose a gift, and hear the news
Little silver bowl
A small copy of the silver mixing bowl with a gold rim that Menelaus gave Telemachus. The real one was the work of Hephaestus.
Helen knew Telemachus at once by his likeness to his father. Menelaus said he would give him three horses and a fine chariot.
Telemachus answered that rocky Ithaca had no wide meadows for horses. Menelaus laughed, liked him for it, and gave him a silver mixing bowl instead.
Then Menelaus told what the Old Man of the Sea had told him on Pharos: that Odysseus was alive, held by the nymph Calypso.
The Old Man of the Sea
As Menelaus: hide under a sealskin, seize Proteus, and hold on through every shape
A scrap of the fresh sealskin Eidothea gave you to hide under. It smells of the sea (and worse).
Menelaus was stuck twenty days on Pharos with no wind. Eidothea, Proteus' daughter, took pity on him.

She hid him and three men under fresh sealskins, and put sweet ambrosia under their noses against the smell. At noon Proteus came up, counted his seals, counted the men among them without noticing, and lay down.
They seized him and held on while he became a lion, a serpent, a leopard, a great boar, running water and a tall tree, until he gave up and answered.

go back aboard, then sail for
The Wooden Horse. Ten years of war, and Troy still stands. Epeius has built a great hollow horse of fir. Climb inside with the best of the Greeks; the rest of the army sails out of sight.
climb into the horse
keep silent in the dark
Inside the horse. It is dark and hot. Thirty men sit knee to knee, swords across their laps. Through a crack you can hear the Trojans dragging the horse up into their city, singing.

A woman's voice outside, calling softly. She is calling each man by name, in the voice of his own wife. It is Helen. "Come down… it's me…" Beside you, young Anticlus opens his mouth to answer. Stay silent…
Night. Helen has gone; Troy is asleep after its feast. You climb down a rope from the horse's belly. Open the gates for the army, which has sailed back in the dark.
climb up into its belly
Helen is calling, in your wife's voice
A hard hand clamps over your mouth: Odysseus. "Not a sound." Helen's voice drifts away… and comes back. Try again: stay silent , whatever she says.
lift the great bar and open them
The gates swing open. The Greek army pours in from the plain, and by morning the ten-year war is over. Now Odysseus has only one wish: to go home to Ithaca. It will take him ten more years.
The Lotus-Eaters. You sent three men inland to see who lives here. They have not come back. Find them, and bring them to the ship; and be careful what you eat.
bring them to the landing
Honey-sweet… while you smile at nothing, your men drift back to the lotus groves.
take him by the arm
weeps and begs to stay, but comes, stumbling, at your side.
A smiling lotus-eater holds out a honey-sweet fruit
Honey-sweet. Why did you come here? It doesn't seem to matter… (it will wear off)
tie them under the rowing benches and sail at once
All three are aboard, tied under the benches, still weeping for the lotus.
Nobody's Escape. You row over to the island with twelve men and a goatskin of very strong wine. Up the slope is a great cave, full of cheeses and pens of lambs. Nobody is home.
make him drunk: three bowls
get out of the cave
His huge hands stroke the ram's back. "Dear ram, why last of the flock today? Grieving for your master's eye?" He lets it pass.
Out! You let go of the fleece, untie your men from under the other rams, and drive the flock down to the ship.
A huge hand gropes along the doorway and sweeps you back into the dark. He is feeling everything that passes. Go out the way a sheep would.
go in with your men
Polyphemus stirs up his fire and sees you. "Strangers! Who are you?"
Polyphemus the Cyclops
